chunks: Ahmad ibn Muhammad narrated from Muhammad ibn Isma'il, from Yunus ibn Ya'qub, from Mu'awiya ibn 'Ammar, who said:

I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about a man from the people of knowledge regarding the truth, who brings me 'bukhtaj' (a type of drink) and says it has been cooked until two-thirds have evaporated, while I know that he drinks it when only half has evaporated. He said: 'It is wine, do not drink it.' I said: 'And what about a man who is not from the people of knowledge, whom we do not know, who drinks it when one-third has evaporated and does not consider it permissible when half has evaporated? He informs us that he has 'bukhtaj' with one-third remaining, having lost two-thirds, and it is drinkable from it.' He said: 'Yes.'

key_terms.بُخْتُج: Bukhtaj (a type of drink, often wine or cider)
key_terms.طُبِخَ: Cooked/boiled (referring to evaporation of water content)

ai.seo_question: What is the ruling on drinking a fermented beverage if the narrator's personal consumption habits contradict their claim of its purity?
ai.summary: This hadith illustrates the Shia legal principle of 'istihsan' (juristic preference) applied to the testimony of a trustworthy person ('ahl al-ma'rifa'), where their known personal practice overrides their verbal claim regarding the evaporation of wine. It highlights the distinction between the testimony of the knowledgeable, whose habits are scrutinized for consistency, and the general public, whose statements are accepted at face value unless proven otherwise. This ruling underscores the practical application of reliability in determining the permissibility of fermented beverages in daily life.
